title: Parried again. He fears the lancet of my art as I fear that of his. The cold steelpen.
html_source:
There is possibly an echo of the fencing scene from Hamlet in the word “parried”.

More generally, however, this plays with a common metaphor of seeing the writer’s pen as a kind of weapon. Stephen’s interior monologue here recognises that Mulligan’s moments of kindness and conciliation are not necessarily genuine, but in fact indicate an anxiety about his eventual representation in the later writings of Stephen Dedalus. If you take Mulligan as a definite counterpart to Oliver St John Gogarty, it seems that this anxiety was warranted. Joyce’s art is concentrated in his “cold steelpen”, an object that suggests the dispassionate recording of what really happened (the coldness, the cold eye) while also being something that could cut and injure as a dagger.

The lancet of Mulligan’s art might well be the surgical instruments he uses as a medical student, which perhaps make Stephen wary. There are doubtless many other suggestions for what Mulligan’s own lancet might be in this case, however.
